Product teams run experiments constantly, and the analyst is the one who reads them. Split the users at random, show one half the old version and the other half the new one, and measure what changes. That's an A B test. This round is about measuring the right thing, and reading the result without fooling yourself. There are nineteen questions. Fifteen get a full answer with the numbers on screen, and the last four go quickly. It starts before any test, with what you measure.

Question one. What makes a good metric? It's specific, measurable, tied to the outcome you care about, and sensitive enough to move when the product does. Prefer rates to counts, because a count also moves with traffic. And it should be hard to game. Specific matters most. Here are three reasonable definitions of an active user, on the same events, and by December they disagree by a factor of three. Question two. What's the difference between a primary, a guardrail, and a vanity metric? The primary metric is the one the change is meant to move, like checkout conversion. A guardrail must not get worse along the way: page speed, refunds, unsubscribes. A vanity metric looks good and decides nothing, like total registered users. Choose the primary and the guardrails before the test starts. Question three. What is a north star metric? One number for the long-term value the product delivers, that every team lines up behind, like weekly active teams for collaboration software. It keeps the day-to-day metrics pointed at durable value. Next, where users drop out.
